> The proposed change sets these options as an odd duck in the repo. (I believe) all other options are encapsulated in dedicated objects, as opposed to the runtime options which will now be a dict only. I wonder if instead we should just un-deprecate (de-deprecate? precate :)?) the class, since it seems like we now need it again.

Good point - although as counter, runtime options (as a concept) are already treated [as a dict](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/blob/main/qiskit_ibm_runtime/options/options.py#L86) to some degree.

Part of the original story was evaluating whether the options were in use, and the main goal of this PR is mostly avoiding the `Warning` being emitted during the normal flow of operations. I'll re-issue the PR focusing on that (keeping it declared as deprecated, but not emitting the warning) and consider that removing the class will be part of a bigger refactor related to options later on.

> but this example suggests that RUNNING may include other preparation stages before the QPU begins executing.

That is indeed the current behavior. The `RUNNING` status indicates that the job was picked up from the queue and is being prepared for execution on the QPU. There is a degree of parallelism in this process, so the time it takes the job to actually make it to the QPU could vary.

> * Maybe there is a fix that needs to be made so that the status returns `CANCELLED`?
> 

`qiskit-ibm-runtime` uses `state.status` and reason code to map the status:

https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/blob/d30ce01a692bba3e296c5c52f58c5ff7d6bdd9c5/qiskit_ibm_runtime/runtime_job_v2.py#L176-L182


`Cancelled - Ran Too Long` is _not_ a documented `state.status`. This is a server-side error and should be fixed on the server-side, not in the client. And a server-side fix would also benefit all versions of qiskit-ibm-runtime.

Considering this PR a feature removal (as in, the `max_execution_time` attribute is removed), I think this is the most relevant bit of the deprecation policy:
> * A deprecation warning must be issued prior to any removal. The warning must indicate what the alternative path is, and the alternative path must be in place when the warning is issued. [...]

where the alternative path is the `max_usage` attribute (introduced at the same time). All in all, the goal is to allow users to use the new attribute and transition (the parent issue is time-sensitive), while still allowing ample time for using the old attribute (ie. no rush in removing the deprecation), in line with the guiding principles.

By "local mode" do you mean running on a fake backend?

We have a [documented](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/local-testing-mode) local testing mode, and the goal is for users to be able to switch between a real QPU and a simulator  (e.g. a fake backend) with only 1 line code change (`backend=`). We didn't quite accomplish that goal because we couldn't support the error mitigation methods, but it's still useful for basic verification. 

Supporting it in wrapper sampler should be very easy - it should just need to check if the `backend` is a simulator and call the existing code.

A few suggestions/preliminary thoughts (cc @diego-plan9)

- I would consider adding a `progress_bar` argument to `SamplerV2.run` that allows users to choose whether or not they want to visualize the progress bar. It could be a bool (ON or OFF) or a literal ("none", "basic", "detailed"), and I'd set it to OFF/"none" by default.
- About the steps to highlight:
  - `Sampler.run` has two main steps: `prepare` and `run`. Both of them should be highlighted.
  - In `prepare` we loop through the PUBs.
      - At the very least, I would signal that we are processing PUB 1, and now we are processing 2, and now 3, ... 
      - Additionally, we can consider providing more fine-grained info ("PUB 1: now doing DD pass manager.. now building template/samplex..")
  - It would be nice to find a solution that allows us to keep the code clean, adding few lines of code. So what I was thinking was a `ProgressBar` class that:
      - knows the "default_level" selected by the user (ON/OFF or the literal)
      - can track progress
      - supports `bar.show(level, "my message")`, which shows the progress bar only if `level >= default_level`; this allows us to add a single line of code per call in `prepare`, and delegates all `if the user wants to see the bar; else ...` to the class itself

> I think we can use the data type of the array to infer the measurement level instead of adding another field to the passthrough data?

I actually think it's generally, and also here, more robust to specify explicitly, while adding some redundancy, rather than inferring one thing from another. It will be possible to distinguish between `kerneled` and `kerneled_avg`, but  will involve adding more code that will bug-prone. For both `kerneled` and `kerneled_avg` the data type is complex numbers, and the dispatch can be done via the array shape.

Any reason to refrain from adding a field? We can exploit the redundancy by asserting that the specified measurement level matches the array's shape and data type.

This PR is the low-tech approach, using just logging facilities, on purpose. I prefer to think of `qiskit-ibm-runtime` as a library first, and keep the spirit as close to it as possible (with visualization and advanced UI belonging to higher levels such as the previous qiskit jupyter widgets, or to user land). 

If we want to move into the direction of a more rich user interface, I would also prefer to introduce it in a more planned way (for example, looking at other instances where long-running operations might benefit from visual indications to the user) instead of a single occurrence for an experimental feature. Implementation-wise, I do agree with the concern (and believe that a non-invasive way of incorporating it can be achieved - with some debate over touching the `run()` signature as technically we are constrained by the base class).
